TL;DR: Game has issues with a lack of Quality-of-life features and end game grind, and if you're aiming to get 100% achievements; then avoid this game. I'm serious. 
(Read below under the 'Getting 100% Steam Achievements' header as to why.)

========================================================================

[h1] POSITIVES [/h1]
[olist]
[*] Characters fall into certain roles, but have some flexibility when fully maxed out and can multi-role pretty well. 

[*] Some of the minigames and side missions are pretty fun and provide useful rewards.

[*] If you're just aiming to reach the end of the story, then you won't have much difficulty.
[/olist]

[h1] NEGATIVES [/h1]
[h2][u] I will talk about my issues regarding getting 100% Steam Achievements in the next header, so none of those issues will appear in this section.[/u][/h2]

[olist]
[*] Since this was a Flash game, the graphics don't exactly hold up well. I'm talking about low quality sprites during the battle screen and how enemies only have one sprite, no variations. So they will slide across the screen when patrolling and don't have any animations when in battle.

[*] Clutter: Once you max out your characters, you'll have so much clutter of Skills to cycle through in battle. The skills do get sorted into specific categories, but even then, some skills feel misplaced like the Poison skill isn't considered a Physical attack, a Magic skill, but a Nerf (Debuff) skill. Not to mention that if you want to search through all acquired skills uncategorized, you're looking at around twelve menus.

[*] Skills: This one is absolutely infuriating. So the healer character I started off with [b][u]CANNOT ACCESS THE STRONGER VARIANT OF THE BASIC FULL PARTY HEAL SPELL[/u][/b] , they're stuck with the basic version. The other party members are also affected by not having skills that would greatly benefit them. You want to know why this is? When investing into stat points into their skill tree, the skills provided for them seems to be randomized (I genuinely hope this is the case, otherwise it's such a horrible decision). So my rogue and speedster party members had access to the stronger full party heal, but not my healer.

[*] Money farming: I spent so much time just replaying the same side mission to grind for coins just to add a few levels to gear upgrades. It takes an absurd amount of coins to max out just one character's gear to beat the hardest bosses. There is no 'easy' method to get coins easily, just grinding away and selling loot which helps, but isn't enough to justify the costs needed for end game upgrades.
[/olist]

[h1] Getting 100% Steam Achievements [/h1]

[olist]
[*] Snowboard Extreme is maddening to achieve. You need to memorize the static areas of the map and have fast reaction speed to get through the randomized zones. You are only allowed to lose five seconds worth of a mistake, which is either once or twice, any more and you will go over the time limit necessary to get this achievement. You will need to play near flawlessly to reach the sub-one minute and twenty second time needed.

[*] Card Class GM: You either end up with opponents who hand you an easy win or you get paired with one whose cards hard-counter yours, and if the game decides that your element swap actually benefits the opponent, you're S.O.L. and without grinding away at the later zones to get specific cards (White Shell and Flame/Wind Samurai), you aren't going to reach 5 wins easily without RNG throwing you an easy win.

[*] Doom Bringer: If you didn't accept the side-mission post-game to retrieve stolen ship parts and fought the boss, guess you're redoing this fight a second time and that sucks, why? Because this boss requires a guide to beat, and it's mindnumbingly boring. Refer to the issue of grinding coins from the above header, because that's what'll take the most time of your 100% achievement run outside of the card minigame.

[*] Generic Quest: Requires a guide, you will never figure out how to achieve this normally with the amount of zones you won't visit outside of initially exploring them. 

[*] Number One Card! and Impossible Deck: There is no useful information about how to get these two because discussion on them is either vague and users don't provide anything helpful or had no replies. Had to look up a YouTube video on this minigame and copied the card layout there to actually advance progress to get these last two achievements. 
[/olist]

Crystal Story II on Steam actually comes with its predecessor, Crystal Story 1. Since I didn't play either, this review covers both games.

Crystal Story 1 graphics was simple and the story was shallow, but what carried the game was that you could customize almost every aspect of your character, and you had all the resources in the world to do so; you could upgrade different types of equipment to suit your characters, spam SP reset to play around with the different types of abilities that each character had etc.

What made Crystal Story 1 phenomenally engaging however, were the characters. You don't get a lot of cutscenes, the story was stupidly absurd, the characters were absolutely comical. It doesn't take itself seriously, the characters don't take themselves or the story seriously, and that makes the game both entertaining and engaging, a rare trait in a lot of games these days.

The characters in Crystal Story 2 didn't have this charm; the story was only a little bit more fleshed out than the first, but the characters took it much more seriously, losing the charm that Crystal Story 1 had. You couldn't respec your points, so if you had specialized your character as a physical damage dealer, you could twist and turn a little to make them deal magical damage later on, but it'll take a while. I feel that Crystal Story 2 had more to offer in terms of game mechanics, but in terms of how engaging the game was, I preferred Crystal Story 1.

That being said, this game is really cheap. Definitely good to pick up and have fun with.

I tried this out on Kongregate many years ago and decided to play it on steam to get the soundtrack and bonus content.

After completing both games and finishing the post-game content, I can safely say that the only true post-post-game content that can genuinely provide endless entertainment is the Zombie Defense mode in Crystal Story I.

The frantic and frenetic twist on the simple match-3 game format is really exciting and evokes feelings of stress, followed by extreme satisfaction once done. The fast paced 8-bit theme also adds to the atmosphere of this small segment of the game and is really catchy too.

It's legitimately the only reason I played the game again and decided to write this review.

Its counterpart in Crystal Story II would probably be the Mercenary Defense mode, which I feel has a lot of potential that goes unused. A small campaign with a few extra bonus challenges at the side would have been nice. The music isn't as catchy and the repeatable final mission feels repetitive after playing for a while.

Overall, a good game with even better minigames.

[h1] 5/10 "It's just okay" is pretty good for a $3 game. [/h1]

Crystal Story 2 is a turn-based, party oriented, class-centric JRPG which can be readily compared to titles such as the early Final Fantasy games (7 and previous) and Final Fantasy Tactics.

[b] The good [/b]

[list]
[*] There are just enough classes in the game (6 in total) to allow for baseline theory crafting. 
[*] The number of skills in the game is pretty low, but [i] most [/i] skills are worth having even on classes that they're not amazing on. 
[*] Equipment availability is just varied enough to provide some meaningful choice options, and the equipment upgrade system means your early game loot can compete later on. 
[*] Stat growths are defined by class, not character, so any party member can potentially fill any role. Your protagonist is not fated to be an unga bunga, and your shooty girl is not required to be a burn mage. Unique weapons in the game can further cement the archetype you want.
[/list]

[b] The bad [/b]

[list]
[*] Tooltips are severely lacking in all areas. The worst is on the level-up screen, where you're given a preview of what skills a class has access to. You are not told what these skills do, exactly, until you cement your class choice. Many times these are self-evident, such as "Heal" or "Attack Down," but the difference between "Water" and "Blizzard" is less apparent. What does "Berserk" do? There is no way to know what you're agreeing to until after you've done it.
[*] Debuffs that aren't slow or poison are worthless. In any fight that matters, vis a vis boss fights, the thing you're trying to debuff will resist status effects about 60-70% of the time. You could do thousands of damage with a character in the time it takes to apply a single debuff, and by which point the rest of your party has nearly killed the enemy anyway, rendering debuffs pointless. Moreover, most bosses have multiple phases. Each phase change purges buffs and debuffs on that unit, so the status you spent 5 turns applying has to be done again. It's just not worth it.
[*] Skill balance. Poison is the strongest ability in the game. Period. You cast it once at the start of a fight and an enemy takes tons of damage for free forever after. Unlike all other debuffs, poison status seems basically guaranteed to land against anything not outright immune, which is basically nothing.
[*] Mob balance. Room battles are pushover easy, and bosses are either a walk or very hard. There were only two boss fights in the entire game that I felt were tough without being impossible. Weenie fights on the map are just chaff to be cut. They exist to be a light show for your skills, which is fine if you're into that but it has the same level of engagement as a game of Bejeweled, which brings me to...
[*] Actual bloody Bejeweled in this game. Why?
[*] It's not clear how much any given skill will delay your next turn. You can see how this could be a problem if you're trying to get an extra action in before the big bad hits you again.
[*] Class variety. There are 6 total classes in the game and you have 4 characters, who get 2 of these classes per level. This means you will take at least two classes twice on your party per level. It makes characters start to feel a little samey as the game progresses, as there is really only one build path for physical, magic, and healing.
[*] The story is about as generic "gather 4 crystals and defeat the big bad" as it comes. The game has nothing to say and none of the narrative is original or fulfilling. Skip it entirely and play for the combat engine.
[/list]

[b] The verdict [/b]

Crystal Story 2 costs $3. Yes, it needs work to be good, but at $3 it doesn't [i] need [/i] to be good. It's okay, and that's okay. You'll enjoy the 10-15 hours you get out of it, but you probably won't remember it fondly 5 years down the line as you will something like Slay the Spire. I would 100% recommend this title at its current price point.
